title: Unauthorized Fire: The Death of Nadab and Abihu
summary: On the day the priesthood begins, Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire before the LORD, and fire from the LORD consumes them. Moses forbids Aaron and his remaining sons to mourn in public or leave the sanctuary, and the LORD tells Aaron that priests must not drink wine when they serve, so that they can distinguish the holy from the common and teach Israel. The chapter ends with a dispute over a sin offering that was burned instead of eaten, settled by Aaron's reply.
story: Chapter 9 ended in joy, with fire from the LORD accepting the offerings and the people shouting and falling on their faces. Chapter 10 happens on the same day. Two of the new priests take their censers, and the same fire comes out and kills them. The Bible often follows a new beginning with a sudden failure: Adam and Eve in the garden, Noah after the flood, the golden calf at the foot of Sinai, Achan after Jericho, and Ananias and Sapphira in the first days of the church. Each time the story shows that the gift of God's presence does not make his people safe from themselves. Nadab and Abihu were not minor figures. They were Aaron's eldest sons (Exodus 6:23), and they had gone up Sinai with Moses and the elders and seen the God of Israel (Exodus 24:9-11). Their deaths overshadow what follows. The Day of Atonement instructions in chapter 16 begin by recalling them, and they explain how the high priest may come near without dying.
historical:
The chapter's people come from the priestly family tree in Exodus 6. Aaron and Elisheba had four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar (Exodus 6:23). Mishael and Elzaphan, who carry out the bodies, were sons of Uzziel, the brother of Aaron's father Amram (Exodus 6:18, 22), which makes them cousins of the dead men; Levites who were not priests could carry them without the priests on duty becoming unclean. Numbers 3:4 adds that Nadab and Abihu died childless, so the priesthood continued through Eleazar and Ithamar alone.

Incense offering had a dangerous history in Israel. The incense altar was not to receive any unauthorized incense (Exodus 30:9), and later stories repeat the lesson. When Korah and his followers challenged Aaron's priesthood, 250 men offering incense were consumed by fire from the LORD (Numbers 16:35). Centuries later King Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense, a task reserved for priests, and was struck with a skin disease that lasted until his death (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). In each case the sin was an attempt to approach God on one's own terms.
cultural:
A censer was a pan for carrying live coals, on which incense was sprinkled to produce fragrant smoke. The proper source of coals was the altar itself (compare 16:12). Where Nadab and Abihu took their fire from, and exactly what made it unauthorized, the text does not say. The bodies were carried out still in their tunics (verse 5), which suggests that the fire killed them without consuming their priestly clothes.

Letting the hair hang loose and tearing one's garments were the ordinary signs of grief. Aaron and his remaining sons are forbidden to make them (verse 6), because they are still under the anointing and in the middle of their service, and later law forbids the high priest to mourn in this way at all (21:10-12). The rest of Israel is told to mourn, so the grief is real and permitted, but it is carried by the people on the priests' behalf. The ban on wine and strong drink (verse 9) ties the priests' clear heads to their two tasks: to tell holy from common and clean from unclean, and to teach Israel God's statutes. Teaching was always part of the priest's work (Deuteronomy 33:10), and Malachi later insists that “the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge” (Malachi 2:7).
literary: The chapter is built on contrasts with the ones before it. Chapters 8 and 9 repeat that everything was done as the LORD commanded; verse 1 says the fire was offered contrary to his command, literally that which he had not commanded them. The fire that came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the offering in 9:24 comes out in the same words and consumes the priests in 10:2. The people shouted in 9:24; here Aaron is silent (verse 3). Moses quotes a two-line saying of the LORD, “To those who come near Me I will show My holiness, and in the sight of all the people I will reveal My glory,” which interprets the event. The chapter then moves through four scenes: the deaths and their aftermath (1-7), the LORD speaking to Aaron alone, one of the few such speeches in the Torah (8-11), instructions about the priests' portions (12-15), and the dispute over the goat of the sin offering (16-20). That dispute ends unusually. Moses is angry, Aaron answers, and Moses accepts the answer.

outline.t: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire and die
The bodies removed; the priests forbidden to mourn
No wine on duty: distinguishing and teaching
The priests' portions of the offerings
The burned sin offering and Aaron's answer

doctrines.note: Nearness to God is a gift that cannot be handled carelessly. The saying in verse 3 links holiness and glory: God shows himself holy among those who come near him, whether in acceptance or in judgment. The priests' task in verse 10 is to guard that same line between holy and common.

Judgment falls hardest on those closest to God and at the moment of greatest privilege. The same fire that accepts worship consumes those who presume on it. The New Testament echoes the principle when it says it is time “for judgment to begin with the family of God” (1 Peter 4:17).

Priests were not only ritual officials but teachers. Verses 10-11 make their clear judgment the condition for Israel's instruction. A people's grasp of God's ways depended on leaders who could tell the difference between holy and common and explain it.

words.note: Zur, to be strange or foreign. The fire of verse 1 is zarah, unauthorized or strange, meaning outside what God had prescribed. The same word describes the unauthorized incense forbidden on the incense altar (Exodus 30:9) and, elsewhere, a foreigner or an outsider to the priestly family. The problem is not that the fire was chemically different but that it did not come on God's terms.

Damam, to be silent or still. Aaron's silence in verse 3 has been read in several ways: stunned grief, submission to God's judgment, or the silence of a man with nothing to say. The same verb appears in the psalms for quiet waiting on God. The text reports it without comment, and the restraint is part of its force.

Badal, to separate or distinguish. It is the verb used in Genesis 1 when God separates light from darkness and the waters above from the waters below. The priests are to continue that ordering work by separating holy from common and clean from unclean (verse 10), and the next chapter applies it to animals (11:47).

christ: Hebrews takes the lesson of this chapter seriously: Christians are to worship God “with reverence and awe,” for “our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28-29). Yet the same letter says believers may now come near with confidence, because they come through a high priest who approached God perfectly on their behalf: “Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence” (Hebrews 4:16). Nadab and Abihu came near on their own terms and died; the New Testament presents Jesus as the priest who came near on God's terms and opened a way for others, “the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body” (Hebrews 10:20). The pattern of a sudden judgment at a new beginning returns in Acts 5, where Ananias and Sapphira die for lying to the Holy Spirit in the church's first days and “great fear came over the whole church.” These parallels are thematic rather than predictive, but they show that the holiness of God in Leviticus 10 is the same holiness Christians meet in Christ.

hard.q: Why were Nadab and Abihu killed for what looks like a ritual mistake?
hard.a:
The text gives only one explanation: they offered fire “contrary to His command” (verse 1). Interpreters since ancient times have tried to specify the fault. Some think the fire did not come from the altar, where the coals were supposed to be taken. Some think they entered further into the sanctuary than they were allowed, since chapter 16 recalls their deaths when it limits entry to the Most Holy Place. Some connect the wine rule of verse 9 to the story and suggest they were drunk. Others see pride or a bid for leadership, acting on their own initiative on the very day the priesthood began. The text leaves the details open, perhaps because the core issue is the same in every case: they treated God's presence as something they could approach however they chose.

The severity also belongs to the moment. At the founding of Israel's worship, the boundary between God's holiness and human presumption had to be clear, and the priests, who stood closest to it, were held to the highest standard. The Bible shows similar judgments at other founding moments, with Uzzah and the ark (2 Samuel 6:6-7) and Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5). Such judgments are rare, and they are never presented as God's normal way with his people, whose ordinary failures the offerings of chapters 4 and 5 were given to cover. Leviticus also refuses to make the grief small. The whole house of Israel is told to mourn.

questions: Nadab and Abihu had seen God on Sinai and still acted presumptuously. Why do privilege and familiarity with holy things sometimes make people careless?
Aaron was silent before God's judgment and later spoke honestly to Moses about his grief. What can we learn from both his silence and his words?
The priests needed clear heads to distinguish holy from common and to teach. What dulls your ability to see those distinctions?
